Bhadariya Excavation.title: Bhadariya Excavation
Bhadariya Excavation.details:
Discovered on the banks of the Chandan River near Amarpur block in Banka district during Chhath Puja preparations, Bhadariya has emerged as one of Bihar's most significant archaeological discoveries in recent years.

Key Excavation Discoveries:
- Structural remains of burnt brick walls, terracotta ring wells, and ancient pottery dating back over 2,600 years (6th century BCE).
- Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR) survey conducted by IIT Kanpur experts to map subsurface structures without destruction.
- Historical links to Buddhist literature mentioning Lord Buddha's visit to the region and the residence of his devout disciple Visakha near Mandar Hill.

Government & BHDS Mandate:
- Chief Minister Nitish Kumar inspected the site and directed comprehensive excavation and riverbed restoration by the Bihar Heritage Development Society (BHDS) and ASI to preserve this ancient Gangetic civilization hub.

Lal Pahari Excavation.title: Lal Pahari Excavation
Lal Pahari Excavation.details:
Situated atop the Lal Pahari hill in Lakhisarai, this site represents the first scientifically excavated hilltop Buddhist monastery (Mahavihara) in Bihar, jointly excavated by the Bihar Heritage Development Society (BHDS) and Visva-Bharati University, Santiniketan.

Architectural & Epigraphic Significance:
- Inscribed clay seals recovered from the excavation bear the legend 'Srimad-Dharmavihar-Arya-Bhikshu-Sanghasya', officially confirming the monastery's historical name.
- Features cella, central shrine, wooden structures, terracotta plaques, and decorative molded bricks reflecting Pala dynasty patronage.
- Uniquely documents the prominence of female Buddhist monks and patrons within the monastic hierarchy of medieval Magadha.

Heritage Protection:
- Declared a protected state monument, ongoing conservation by BHDS aims to preserve the structural walls and develop a dedicated site interpretation center.

Lari Mound Exploration.title: Lari Mound Exploration
Lari Mound Exploration.details:
Located in the Kurtha region (historically part of greater Jehanabad district), Lari features a massive 27-acre archaeological mound that preserves over two millennia of continuous human settlement.

Key Exploration Finds:
- Continuous occupational sequence spanning Pre-Mauryan, Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), Mauryan, Gupta, and Pala historical periods.
- Surface explorations and soil sampling yielded ancient punch-marked coins, terracotta ring wells, clay sealings, iron artifacts, and residential brick walls.
- Significant evidence of early urban planning and craftsmanship in ancient Magadha along regional trade corridors.

Ongoing Research:
- Explorations and survey initiatives by the Bihar Heritage Development Society (BHDS) aim to map the full extent of the mound and secure permanent protection under archaeological preservation acts.

Kutumba Garh Exploration.title: Kutumba Garh Exploration
Kutumba Garh Exploration.details:
Kutumba Garh in the Kutumba/Amba block of Aurangabad district is a historic fort mound site recognized for its deep archaeological potential and strategic location in south-western Bihar.

Archaeological Highlights:
- Uncovered remnants of ancient brick fortifications, structural walls, terracotta figurines, and stone sculptures reflecting Gupta and post-Gupta craftsmanship.
- Yielded historical inscriptions and coins pointing to a fortified administrative and military stronghold in early medieval Magadha.
- Surface explorations and trenching by Bihar State Archaeology and BHDS have identified multi-period cultural deposits.

Development & Conservation:
- Highlighted by state heritage authorities for expanded scientific excavation and inclusion in Bihar's archaeological tourism itinerary.

Nalanda University.title: Nalanda University
Nalanda University.details:
Nalanda University, founded in the 5th century CE, was a prominent center of learning in ancient India, attracting scholars and students from across Asia. It flourished for over 800 years under the Pala dynasty. Renowned for its vast library and diverse curriculum, Nalanda was a major hub for Buddhist studies, as well as medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy.

Founding and Early Years:
- Established around 427 CE by Emperor Kumaragupta I.
- Functioned as a mahavihara, combining religious study with secular subjects.

Peak of Influence:
- Reached its zenith in the 7th–9th centuries CE (was already at its height when Xuanzang visited in the 7th century).
- Hosted an estimated 10,000 scholars and students.
- Library housed millions of palm-leaf manuscripts.

Notable Scholars:
- Aryabhata is traditionally associated with Nalanda, though direct historical evidence that he studied or taught there is inconclusive.
- Covered subjects like Ayurveda, astronomy, grammar, and Buddhist philosophy.

Decline:
- Experienced a gradual process of decline under the Sena dynasty, culminating in destructive attacks during the invasion of Bakhtiyar Khilji in the late 12th century.

Modern Revival:
- Recently revived on a new campus including sustainable, net-zero infrastructure.

Vikramashila.title: Vikramashila
Vikramashila.details: Founded by Pala emperor Dharmapala around the late 8th century CE at Antichak near Bhagalpur, Vikramashila was one of the great Buddhist mahaviharas of its time, specializing in Vajrayāna (Tantric Buddhism). The fortified complex comprised six colleges, a central stupa, and 108 small temples. It housed over 100 teachers and 1,000 students, including the notable scholar Atiśa. The monastery operated under a structured hierarchy, including an abbot, six gate scholars, panditas, and bhikṣus. It thrived as an international center of Buddhist learning until its destruction by Bakhtiyar Khalji’s forces around 1193 CE. Its scholars continued to influence Buddhist traditions in Tibet and Sri Lanka.

Patliputra.title: Patliputra
Patliputra.details: Developed from the fortified settlement established by King Ajatashatru around 490 BCE at the confluence of the Ganges, Son, and Gandak rivers, and later made the capital by King Udayin, Patliputra spanned roughly 2.5 km × 15 km and was fortified with wooden palisades, boasting 64 gates and an estimated 570 towers. Excavations at Kumhrar revealed an 80-pillared hall once part of a grand palace; Bulandi Bagh exposed massive wooden walls and the famed Pataliputra capital (a 3rd-century BCE sandstone artifact now in Patna Museum); Agam Kuan, a brick-lined well (≈32 m deep), is linked to Ashokan lore. During the Mauryan period (3rd century BCE), Patliputra was one of the world’s largest cities, rich in gold-adorned architecture, gardens, stone pillars, and ponds. It remained the seat of successive dynasties (Haryanka, Nanda, Maurya, Shunga, and Gupta) until decline set in by the 7th century, when Xuanzang described it as largely in ruins.

Rohtasgarh Fort.title: Rohtasgarh Fort
Rohtasgarh Fort.details: Perched ~1,500 ft atop the Kaimur hills overlooking the Son River, Rohtasgarh has roots as early as the 7th century, when the Gauda king Shashanka inscribed the site. By 1223 CE, it belonged to the Khayaravala ruler Śrī-Pratāpa, who repelled a Muslim army. In 1539, Sher Shah Suri captured the fort. According to popular tradition, he gained entry by concealing soldiers in palanquins and later stationed a 10,000-strong garrison there. His general Haibat Khan built the three-domed white sandstone Jami Masjid and mausoleum in 1543. Under Akbar’s general Raja Man Singh (1558), the fort became a Mughal stronghold featuring the four-storied Takht-e-Badshahi palace, Aina Mahal, Persian gardens, ponds, the ornate Hathiya Pol gate (1597), and temples of Ganesh and Shiva. The citadel spans some 70 ha, with over 4 km of sandstone ramparts, 68 bastions, 83 gates, machicolations, and underground passages. Later used by Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan), as a Mughal prison under Aurangzeb, briefly held by the British, and as a rebel bastion during the 1857 uprising, the fort remains in impressive ruins—a testament to Hindu, Afghan, and Mughal legacies, yet largely unrestored.

Rajgir Hills.title: Rajgir Hills
Rajgir Hills.details: Rajgir, ancient Rajagriha, was the early capital of Magadha under Bimbisara (c. 540–491 BCE) and Ajatashatru, enfolded by massive cyclopean walls along five quartzite ridges (elev. ~388 m). It became a focal site of Buddhism and Jainism—Buddha taught at Vulture’s Peak (Gridhrakūṭa), and the Saptaparni Cave hosted the First Buddhist Council. The Son Bhandar Caves contain 3rd–4th century CE Jain inscriptions and are traditionally linked to Bimbisara’s treasures. Mahavira also spent multiple chaturmases here, and numerous ancient Jain temples remain. Archaeological excavations have revealed Bimbisara’s prison, Ajatashatru’s fort, Maniyar Math, and evidence of habitation from the Palaeolithic through the Pala period. At its foot, the Brahmakund hot springs (≈45 °C) are revered for their healing properties. Modern amenities include a ropeway to the Peace Pagoda, hill trails, panoramic views, and cycling paths, making Rajgir both a spiritual and scenic heritage destination.

Telhara Monastery.title: Telhara Monastery
Telhara Monastery.details: Telhara (ancient Telāḍhaka), in Nalanda district, was a major Buddhist Mahāvihāra active from the 1st century CE to the 12th century CE. First described by the Chinese traveller Xuanzang in the 7th century, excavations (2009–14, 2020–22) unearthed a three-storeyed monastery complex, prayer halls, residential cells, and stupas across successive layers from the Northern Black Polished Ware period (3rd century BCE) through the Kushan, Gupta, Pāla, and Sena periods. Over a thousand artefacts—including terracotta monastery seals, pottery, bronze and basalt Buddha statues (in Abhay and Dharmacakra mudrās), rich Pāla-era sculptures, and inscriptions—affirm its links to the Buddhist learning networks of Nalanda. Evidence of a thick ash layer suggests destruction during Bakhtiyar Khilji’s invasion in the late 12th century. Chinese accounts mention seven viharas housing around 1,000 monks. Mentioned in the Ain-i-Akbari as a Mughal pargana, its ruins include a later mosque built using monastery stones. Today, the site remains under excavation, with plans for a site museum and renewed scholarly interest.

Kesaria Stupa Mapping.title: Kesaria Stupa Mapping
Kesaria Stupa Mapping.details: The 32 m–high Kesaria Stupa in East Champaran, Bihar—one of the tallest Buddhist stupas in India—was originally built in the 3rd century BCE under Ashoka and later expanded during the Gupta–Pala periods (~200–750 CE). Recent GIS‑based mapping and ASI excavations (1997–98; Patna Circle and Patna Branch in 2018–19) have revealed its full architectural plan: a 31.5 m high terraced stupa (c. 123 m base diameter) with six concentric circular terraces and a massive base wall, possibly extending the diameter to 167 m. Dozens of cell‑shrines with stucco Buddha figures, ornamental geometric patterns, perimeter moats, pradakshina‑paths (circumambulation walk), and relic casket chambers have been mapped. Additional nearby excavations at the Raniwas mound uncovered an extensive monastic complex—cells, corridors, and stupas—suggesting a functional satellite vihara connected to Kesaria. The combined insights from GIS‑mapping and stratigraphic excavation are reshaping scholarly understanding of large‑scale stupa planning in ancient India.

Sasaram Tombs Documentation.title: Sasaram Tombs Documentation
Sasaram Tombs Documentation.details:
The monumental tomb of Sher Shah Suri in Sasaram, Bihar—often called the “Second Taj”—was built between 1540 and 1545 by Mir Muhammad Aliwal Khan in Indo‑Islamic (Afghan‑Mughal) style. Standing 122 ft tall on a three-tiered octagonal plinth at the center of a 22‑acre artificial lake (approx. 1,130 × 865 ft), it features an elegant full‑height dome (22 m span), chhatris at each corner of the second and third stories, and a surrounding verandah with 24 smaller domes and arched openings.

Carved with Quranic verses and intricate floral motifs, the tomb was originally decorated with glazed tiles in blue and yellow hues—earning it the moniker “Second Taj”. Painted depictions from the 1770s show a pavilion atop the tomb replaced during an 1882–83 renovation by Beglar.

Today, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is actively restoring the site—cleaning the lake and inlet canal, installing solar lighting, landscape beautification, repairing access ways to the top floor (reopening visitor access), and reclaiming encroached land.

Nalanda Digital Reconstruction.title: Nalanda Digital Reconstruction
Nalanda Digital Reconstruction.details: Under the Archaeological Survey of India and the Ministry of Culture, an ongoing effort is underway to digitally restore Nalanda Mahavihara, using 3D modeling, GIS mapping, and AR/VR technologies to recreate its ancient architecture and libraries. A pilot AR/VR visualization project is expected to launch by April, aiming to give visitors an immersive sense of Nalanda’s grandeur as it once stood. GIS-based studies using Cartosat-1 stereo imagery and satellite multispectral data have already mapped the full archaeological extent—revealing outlying ruins far beyond the core area, and integrating historical survey data into a layered spatial model. Combined with ASR-based ground surveys, photogrammetric modeling, public image‑crowdsourcing platforms, and CHIS/AR initiatives like JATAN and virtual museum builders, this work aims to digitally preserve, reconstruct, and reinterpret monastery layouts, stupas, temples, temples halls, and libraries—enhancing onsite visitor experience and enabling academic study.

Vikramshila River Excavation.title: Vikramshila River Excavation
Vikramshila River Excavation.details: Excavations near the ancient river channel adjacent to the Vikramshila Mahavihara—conducted after ASI resumed work in early 2024—have uncovered a wide array of Pala-period artifacts. These include terracotta plaques, human and animal figurines, beads of stone, glass, and terracotta, stone and bronze Buddhist and Hindu images (e.g., Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Manjushri, Tara), seals and sealings, and household pottery and metal finds such as coins and copper rings. The finds suggest river-based trade activity, evidenced by beads and pottery types—alongside votive stupas and stupa remnants—highlighting the site's role in monastic life and commerce during the Pala dynasty.

Rohtasgarh Tunnel Study.title: Rohtasgarh Tunnel Study
Rohtasgarh Tunnel Study.details: Recent archaeological work at Rohtasgarh Fort—one of India's largest and most extensive hill fort complexes spanning over 42 km² of plateau—has turned scholarly attention to its extensive underground network of tunnels and chambers. According to historical surveys, the fort contains a network of underground tunnels, historically believed to have served as escape routes or secret passageways during sieges. On‑site investigations at the Bada Angana courtyard have revealed hidden stairways leading into vaulted chambers with domes and ventilators, including large underground halls like the ‘Nach‑ghar’ (dancing hall) (~48 × 45 ft) and the ‘Raniwas’ (~59 × 37 ft), hinting at elaborate subterranean planning.

Chausa Excavation.title: Chausa Excavation
Chausa Excavation.details: Excavations and explorations at Chausa near Buxar, celebrated for the landmark 1931 discovery of the Chausa Hoard (18 ancient Jain bronze sculptures dating from the 1st century BCE to the Gupta era), have revealed significant archaeological evidence confirming deep antiquity. Recent archaeological surveys have unearthed coins and seals from the Gupta era (4th–6th century CE), terracotta figurines, and ancient brick foundations, pointing to a well-organized ancient riverine settlement. The site, also famous as the battleground of Humayun and Sher Shah Suri in 1539 CE, demonstrates continuous strategic occupation across ancient and medieval Indian history.
